utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. I wonder whether the Registrar could be so kind as to call out the case number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Case number IT-95-13a-T, the Prosecutor versus Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I have the appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases, my name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues, Mr. Waespi, Ms. Sutherland, Mr. Williamson and Mr. Vos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honour. I am Toma Fila, appearing together with Ms. Lopicic and Mr. Petrovic on behalf of Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask Mr. Dokmanovic whether he can hear me well? Thank you. Now, before the Prosecution calls its first witness for this morning, we would like to raise an issue. The court would like to raise a question about the Prosecution witnesses to be called in March on the exhumation of the mass grave at Ovcara. Our purpose is to see whether we might be able to narrow down the issues in dispute concerning these exhumations. We have noticed that last Friday Mr. Fila said the following. It is in the transcript, page 1003, and I quote: "Regarding the Ovcara questions, the Defence is not denying at all the findings there and that those people were killed at Ovcara. I said yesterday too, and last time, that I am not disputing that there was an armed conflict. What I am disputing is an international armed conflict. I am not disputing that there were 200 bodies found. I am just trying to establish which bodies they were." We therefore wonder whether Mr. Fila could specify what he is putting in issue concerning the mass grave. Mr. Fila, are you still disputing that most of the persons found in the mass grave were taken from the Vukovar hospital on the 19th or 20th November 1991? Before you answer this question, Mr. Fila, let me point out that we are endeavouring to see whether, in March, the Prosecution could tailor their case more specifically so as to address the points disputed by the Defence. It should, however, be clear that the court is in no way trying to push the Prosecution to compress its case unreasonably. So therefore I turn to Mr. Fila, and ask him whether he could answer my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, from the beginning of this trial I am not disputing that what happened in Ovcara is a violations of the Geneva Conventions, that it is a dishonourable and abhorrent act. Even though I belong to the people I belong to, I am ashamed of what has happened at Ovcara, and I hope that that is clear. The reason that the Defence has disputed individual names is in order to try and establish exactly who it was that was left there, and where an error was made, simply because this would be advantageous for the judgement too, to have the accurate data. The second point is that the indictment says that they were all non-Serbs. That is not correct. Among the persons executed at Ovcara there are Serbs and we have listed them. We expect the Prosecutor to prove that they were non-Serbs because the burden is on the Prosecution, and there are four such persons, four names. Secondly, you will see in the reports on the abductions that there is the name of a man who has been identified as executed at Ovcara, OVC 177, but who has not been included in the indictment because it is stated there that he was probably a Serb. So the Defence wonders, if the persons executed were Serbs, does that mean that they should not figure in the indictment? From this, one could make the conclusion that it is permissible to kill Serbs, even at Ovcara, or is it just a question of a mistake? But the only thing I am disputing at Ovcara is that it is not true that only non-Serbs were executed. If the forensic commission has found 200 bodies then it has found 200 bodies, and it is not my intention to dispute that, nor do I have any doubts regarding their findings, and also that most of those 200 bodies are people captured at the hospital, but not only on 20th, but also on the 19th, to which certain witnesses have already testified. I hope I have been clear enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Niemann, I assume you will now respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: In particular also, bearing in mind what we can find in the disclaimer included in the documents of the forensic investigation at Ovcara grave where it is stated that the conclusions of the report are not final because the final overall analysis by the forensic pathologist is not -- is still missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, perhaps I might address that first. That is not tendered and will not be tendered. It is not evidence in the case. It is merely background material which can be made available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Oh, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The position of the Prosecution on this, your Honours, is that we hear what Mr. Fila says, but he is saying two things. He is saying, "yes, yes, we do not dispute that a terrible thing happened at Ovcara", and that, "no doubt this would represent a breach of the Geneva Conventions, if we can prove international armed conflict and so forth", but then he goes often and he says, and has consistently, and we are not criticising him for it, it is his job to do it, but has consistently attacked the indictment on the basis of people named and more recently on the issue of whether or not Serbs were there or not. This is not clear. This is not a matter which can be readily resolved by an admission unless we have a very clear admission in writing as to these matters. We have an obligation to prove murder and proof of the murder is proof of death. I have not heard Mr. Fila say that he accepts that murder was committed, and that the proof, the element of proof of death has been established, and that he will admit to that, and I am not sure that he will. So, it is very difficult to say to the Prosecution, "reduce your case. Mr. Fila agrees to it all", and then at the end of the day we are confronted with an absence of evidence on this issue, so, I mean, we -- we are not trying to prolong this case and indeed I think the opposite is the case. It has proceeded faster than any other prosecution in this Tribunal, and we are endeavouring to be as expeditious as possible, but we have certain obligations, and I am not convinced, certainly, at this stage, that we have a sufficiently extensive and wide enough admission from the Defence to say, "Oh, we can just cut the end of the case off and that will be okay because everybody agrees with it, with the Prosecution contention, agrees that the Prosecution has proved the various elements that it must establish". We say that we have to prove a number of things, and one of the issues raised by Mr. Fila goes to the very heart of the question, and that is the definition of the group attacked. We -- there may well be Serbs in the group. We are not saying that, but we do need to establish that a -- that civilian population was singled out and attacked and that as a consequence of that they ended up being murdered at Ovcara. That is what we are alleging and that is what we are seeking to prove. Now, I do not think that Mr. Fila's admissions go anywhere near that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I accept that 200 people were killed at Ovcara. Whether they were all civilians or not, I do not know, but it is a fact that there were soldiers, as the witnesses have told us, who were intentionally cut, cuts were made on their bodies in order to cover up their condition. You heard that from the doctor, that some people had plaster casts placed on them. Those were not civilians. Those were fighters, Croatian fighters, Zengers, Guards members or whoever. Not for a moment am I denying that what happened in Ovcara is a crime, a murder. What I seek is that we establish that they were not just non-Serbs, that Serbs were murdered as well, and in my opinion, if you kill a civilian, it does not matter whether he is a Serb or a Croat, but it is important that we know, because neither Serbs nor Croats should be murdered. Therefore, I do not know how to make myself clearer. I accept that it is a murder, that it is a breach of the Geneva Conventions during an armed conflict, but I do not accept that they were only civilian prisoners, that they were all from the hospital, and that they were all non-Serbs, so I ask the Prosecutor to prove that those four persons were Croats, or Chinamen, if you like, that they were non-Serbs, in brief, because they were Serbs, and I would like to know why a Serb who has been identified as having been killed at Ovcara is not included in the indictment, and I have indicated the names. I do not know how to make myself clearer than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you mean to say that you admit that those people who were found, whose bodies were found at Ovcara were killed, and -- were executed. However, the dead do not include only Croatian civilians, taken from the hospital to Ovcara, but also non-civilians, and Serbs, whether or not the Serbs were taken from the hospital or not from the hospital. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I do not know where they were taken from because I do not have the list, but that they were killed at Ovcara, that is obvious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: The only point at issue, therefore, in dispute, is whether or not in addition to civilians killed at Ovcara, and brought to Ovcara first of all out of the hospital on 19th or 20th, there were also in Ovcara people who were killed but were not civilian, because they were combatants or Serbs. This is the point in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, no, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, just that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There is a world of difference between someone killed and someone murdered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I used -- you are right. I meant to say, "murdered". I think Mr. Fila before said -- I wrote it down: "I admit there was a murder --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Executed. Executed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, I will only accept murder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Do you accept that --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, I do, completely, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You accept, you admit that those people were murdered at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It depends when we count on the premeditation element. That is the question. When they were brought to Ovcara, I admit they were brought there in order to be executed, if Mr. Niemann is satisfied with that. Is that acceptable?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am afraid not, your Honour. We have to establish murder and if we are not going to call evidence we have to have an admission to murder and it has to be murder, premeditated, from the moment they were taken from the hospital right through to the point where they were shot at the grave site.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, can I make this suggestion in order to try and cut the knot? Clearly, what you are concerned about is that the admissions are not very clear at the moment, and do not necessarily cover all the necessary points.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is right, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, I do not know if it is the procedure here but it would seem to me that one way to deal with it might be this; if you were to draft the admissions which you would require in order to cover the point about the exhumations and murder, they could then be put to the Defence, and it could be ascertained whether the Defence accept the admissions or not, or are prepared to make the admissions. Would that be a way forward?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I am sure that would. If it was agreed then there would be no difficulty. It would be something which I would then seek to tender in the proceedings and we could proceed from there. But I am afraid I am far from satisfied at the moment, because of the various issues that Mr. Fila has quite rightfully raised. I am not in any way critical of Mr. Fila. He is entitled to argue anything he likes in the case but I am not satisfied that they constitute a sufficient admission for us to say, "we do not need to call evidence on it".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If we had your draft of the admissions you would seek, then at least it might serve to narrow the issues, and of course if they were made it would save the calling of the evidence. It would, of course, be entirely a matter for the Defence whether they made the admissions or not. It is entirely for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And I think, your Honours, we would like the admissions to be agreed to, not only by counsel for the Defence but at least some assurance that the defendant himself accepts those admissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Of course. Mr. Fila, what I am suggesting, since Mr. Niemann does not seem to be -- does not seem to be satisfied, and of course it is a matter for him entirely, with the suggested admissions, is that he drafts the admissions which he says that he wants, and you have a copy, and have a look at it and decide whether you could make the admissions or not, of course it being a matter entirely for you, entirely for you, and the defendant, whether those admissions are made. Just as a way of trying to clarify and narrow the issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honours, please bear in mind the delicacy of my position and where I come from. The only thing I cannot accept is that the moment they were taken out of the hospital on 19th and 20th that already a decision had been taken to execute them. What I can accept is that when they were captured, as Witness Q stated yesterday, from the barracks onwards the decision was taken to liquidate them. That I accept, but that such a decision existed already in the hospital I do not accept and cannot accept. And anyway, I must not accept. It is very clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. So you will -- anyway, you are accepting the suggestion made by Judge May and accepted by the Prosecutor that the Prosecutor will prepare this draft of admission and then you will see whether you may accept, after consulting with the defendant. I think, however, this discussion this morning has been extremely useful, at least for the bench, because we have now a clearer idea of the points in dispute. All right. So we may now, if you agree, we may now ask the Prosecutor to call the first witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just with respect to our order of witnesses today, your Honour, the witness, Witness A, is still ill and my colleague, Mr. Williamson intends to take him through his evidence. We are hoping that he will be in a sufficiently healthy or fit enough condition to testify this afternoon, but we believe that if we can give him the morning to endeavour to recuperate he should be okay by this afternoon but there is some uncertainty about that at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. Our next witness will be Mr. Jan Schou and he will testify in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. I would like to ask you to make the solemn declaration. JAN SCHOU (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Mr. Waespi, you may proceed. Examined by MR. WAESPI

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Schou. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please state for the court your name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Dr. Jan Schou.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you interviewed on 4th and 5th of December 1995 by investigators from this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you sign a document which was the written result of this interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will now show you a document and ask you whether this is the document you have signed in December 1995. Do you see your signature on it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like to tender this document as the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 73.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And it should be under seal. Dr. Schou, what nationality are you, and where are you living at present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am Danish, and I am living in Jutland in Denmark.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a specialist in gynaecology.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1991 were you a member of the ECMM, that is European Community Monitoring Mission in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the reason for this assignment? How did you qualify for that job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Danish Foreign Ministry wanted, or the Danish army wanted a military person which also was a doctor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In general, what was your duty, your function within the ECMM structure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was -- well, the medical doctor of the staff of the ECMM members, and then I was in charge of all negotiations about prisoners and evacuations and wounded and something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you based?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was based in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now turning to the fall in 1991, did you participate in two ECMM relief convoys in Vukovar, one in October and one in November 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please give us details about the first mission? I will ask you some questions about that. What was the purpose of this first mission in October 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was to make a humanitarian corridor to Vukovar and to get the wounded out from the hospital. The mission had tried it, I think, two weeks before, but it failed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that convoy, that relief convoy, part of an agreement between the warring parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was an agreement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who were these warring parties? Who were also part of that agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The parties to the agreement were General Raseta from the JNA, and I did not know the name but someone from the Croatian government, and the chief of the EC Monitors, and of course also the NGO Medicine Without Borders, which was our humanitarian partner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Judging from your experience during those negotiations, was the Croatian government an equal partner in these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you depart from Zagreb and when did you arrive in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We departed from Zagreb on 18th October and stayed outside in Negoslavci -- no, Vinkovci, I think, the night over, and at the 19th October we started in morning and reached Vukovar about 12 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a specific route, a way you were required to take?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a specific route and it was Nustar, Marinci, Bogdanovci and then Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you, in fact, follow that route?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We followed that route until we reached Bogdanovci where we were told from the Croatian side that the road was mined, that we had to take another way, and they guided us, the whole convoy which had a lot of ambulances, we were guided through the fields, outside the road and reach Luzac and then Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any incident on that route to which the Croatians directed you to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What situation did you encounter in Vukovar in general, and in the hospital in particular.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We -- travelling directly to the hospital and on the way we saw a lot of buildings which were damaged, and at the hospital we saw that it was damaged and only the basement could be used for “hospitality”.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the hospital defended?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a kind of defence I think there were, because outside there were soldiers from the Croatian -- not the army, I think it was local.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any heavy weapons in the hospital, machine-guns?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not see any heavy weapons in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear at a certain point another type of weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I heard a mortar firing from the hospital area at the time we were in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you the only person in your relief convoy who was able to hear that noise, that weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was the only one that -- I am the only one that had heard it, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. How many patients did you take with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I take about 110 patient.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you leave again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think we leave the same day about three hours before it get dark.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, who formed this convoy when you went back to Zagreb? How many cars, and can you also give us some names of your colleagues, or tell us at least the countries they were from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The leader of the convoy from the ECMM was a French colonel, did not know his name. His name was Pierre, I think, and then there was a Danish captain named is Mesk and I think we were about four or five ECMM cars in that convoy, so at least we were 12 or 13 ECMM member in that that relief convoy, and I was in the first car with the leader and with a Canadian sea officer, and of course the driver. We were four in the car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, heading out of Vukovar, did you take the same route as you had on the way to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We started on the same route with our Croatian guide in front of us in a civilian car, and then our car which was a leading car, and then we have the relief -- no, the relation officer from the Serbs in the car behind, and then we have all the ambulances and trucks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, you tried to get out the same safe way you had entered Vukovar, which was obviously cleared of mines.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were you stopped at some point on the way out of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When we go into the field, again, just outside Luzac, there was a wire across the road, and our leader, he examined the wire and cut it and then we drive further around the corner, and then in front of us there was a T-72 tank from the JNA army which was pointed at the car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you encounter an officer in charge of that tank or the forces you were stopped by?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There were the tanks and then there was an APC that took us to a hill, just beneath where there was an officer in charge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us the name of that officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The name of that officer was Major Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you mean, "Sljivancanin"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what did Mr. Sljivancanin tell you? Did you have any conversation with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You cannot call it a conversation because he had arranged a press conference. At the time we reached the top there were at least three or four television teams with satellite communication that -- and he was almost making a statement there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What exactly did he tell you or the media in his statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He tell us that we were co-operating with the Croatian -- that we were not following the agreement, that we were not following the route we were told to take, and a lot of things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think that this situation, this scene was prepared by --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it was prepared by the JNA because at the time we were stopped, the press already were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Sljivancanin give you then any instruction on how to, which route to take following this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We had to follow the original route back to Bogdanovci, Marinci, Nustar and then Vinkovci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you indicate to him that you were concerned about the fact that the road might be mined?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We told him that we had been told from the Croatian side, that the road was mined.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did he reply?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said that we had to take that way because it was the agreement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you in fact went on to the road Sljivancanin directed you to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the result?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The result was that the fourth car, which was a truck, hit a mine on the road, and two nurses from Switzerland was blowing out of the car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the nurses seriously wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was at least a broken leg but at that time they were unconscious and we only treated them because we did not know what was happened with them. But I hear later that they had lost their hearing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this occurred on the road, Sljivancanin had ordered you to go on. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will now show you a map, depicting the western part of the surroundings of Vukovar. I would like you, Dr. Schou, to show us the locations and roads of this first relief convoy to Vukovar, if you could, please, put it onto the overhead projector and it takes some time, if you could use a pen and indicate, first telling us, as soon as we see it on our screen where the locations are, where Vukovar is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was here. (Indicated).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the general direction of your convoy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Between -- the agreement of the convoy was Nustar, which is just outside here, Marinci, which was on the Serbian side, Bogdanovci, which were JNA -- no, no, this was Serbian side, this was Croatian side, Bogdanovci and then this way to Vukovar. (Indicated).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So can you make with your pen a line and tell us which way you were supposed, according to the agreement, to take when you entered Vukovar. Just what you said in words now, drawing a line.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The agreement were Marinci, Bogdanovci and Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the usher could give you an appropriate pen, please. So first, the road you were supposed to take. Okay. Thank you. Can you please mark it with an "A", capital "A"? Then I would like you to show us the location when you were stopped by the Croatians when you entered Vukovar, and mark it with a, "B", please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then third, on which road were you directed by the Croatians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This way... into the hospital which is here. (Indicated).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is, "C", please, if you could sign it and that was a road which was safe for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was a road which was safe on the way in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, fourth, the way you again wanted to take in order to leave the city which is, I assume --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is this one, C.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. If you could again, please, mark it with a "D", then the location where you were stopped by the JNA and where...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map). We were stopped at this -- something about this point and we were taken to the hill here where the press conference was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, if you could mark that with an, "E", the press conference, and then next the road Sljivancanin directed you to, which was the original road, the first one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was the original road, yes, and then we were stopped by a mine, something like this. (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If you could mark the location of that mine with a, "G". Thank you very much, Dr. Schou. Your Honours, I tender this map as Prosecution exhibit number...

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Dr. Schou, when did you eventually arrived in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From that point where we were stopped by the mine, we were taken by the JNA to Petrovci and then to Sid and the way around, nearly around Bosnia, back to Vinkovci, and we arrived in Zagreb, I think, one day after, because it take the whole night to travel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Let us turn now to the second trip in November 1991. What was the reason for this second trip?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reason, we had a meeting in Zagreb with the Red Cross about evacuation of Vukovar, or try to evacuate Vukovar, but then we heard from the Serbian side that Vukovar was nearly taken, and I was flying with the head of mission to evacuate and from there we had -- we were asked from the ECMM to monitor the -- you can call it the fall of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you depart from Belgrade and who was with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We depart from Belgrade on 19th November in the morning, and there were two ECMM teams with three people in each team and then me as a special -- you can call it, because I was the only doctor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a liaison person from the side of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were two liaison officers from the JNA which we picked up in the military headquarters in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you arrive in the area of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In, I think, about 10 o'clock or something in the morning on the 19th, we arrived just outside Sid where we were stopped by a control post and were not allowed to go further, and the liaison officer, they -- travelling further to reach the headquarters to get permission to -- that we could travel further, but from Belgrade we had permission that we could go to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the reasons why you could not proceed with your mission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. I do not know the reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you eventually go to Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We were waiting, I think about four hours, three or four hours at that checkpoint, and then we were almost returning to Belgrade, but then the relation officer came back and took us to the military headquarters in Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whom did you meet there at those headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At those headquarters I meet Major Sljivancanin again, and I met the colonel which was in charge of the militia JNA in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that a gentleman called Colonel Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, seeing Mr. Sljivancanin again, what was he doing with the army? What was his function, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my opinion, he was a political officer and I said that because in Denmark in the military army I am educated as an intelligence officer and I learn about how headquarters are built up, and Sljivancanin, he had a special uniform, he had a quite new uniform, compared to the normal soldiers there, and the colonel there. He had a -- an used uniform. You could see that he had been out in the sun and there was some dirt on the uniform. So in that way he had special uniform, not special, it was the same but it was quite new uniform, camouflage uniform, and also that the colonel almost had to listen to everything he said, what the major said, so the major was in a kind of charge, but not in charge of the forces, but in charge of everything, what has happened in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a meeting with Sljivancanin and Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we have a meeting there where we try to get an agreement to reach the centre of Vukovar and especially the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That day, the 19th, did you try again to enter the city of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We tried to enter the city of Vukovar and we were taking on a kind of “sightseeing trip” to outside Vukovar where we could see into the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you eventually manage to go into the city?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We go just in the beginning of the city, and we were seeing that there were fighting going on in the city at that time. It was on 19th in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you at some point in time in that afternoon able to call the hospital and to talk to somebody from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. From our car we called the hospital and we reached Dr. Bosanac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe you mean Dr. Bosanac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Bosanac. It was my interpreter which were in the car that were talking with her and she only said that we had to come fast and help the people there. And it was only, I think, 13 seconds or something like that, and then the line was broken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did she give any reason why you had to be fast?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The hospital was nearly taken over by the JNA, or by the -- I do not think she said the JNA, I think she said, "the Serbs".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have the impression she was more concerned about the hospital being taken over or that something might happen to the patients?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was that she was caring about, that something could happen to the patients. She said that it was awful at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear whether the ICRC was able to reach the hospital that afternoon, 19th November?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We hear from the headquarters that the Red Cross in the afternoon, later in the afternoon, reached the hospital and were throwing away again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were thrown away again after having reached...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Turning now to the following morning, the 20th of November 1991, did you again try to get into the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we tried to get into the hospital and we were told at that time in the morning that the hospital was taken over, and that the Dr. Bosanac was captured with some other people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By "Dr. Bosan" you mean Dr. Bosanac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The same person who you had talked on the telephone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the woman who was leader of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you successful this time in reaching the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We reached the bridge over the Vuka in the city, and at that time we were told, and held back for I think two or three hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time in the morning was that around? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It must be about 10 o'clock in the morning or something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far away from the hospital were you stopped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think two kilometres or something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And by whom were you stopped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were stopped by Major Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is the same person you saw giving that press conference about a month ago and again the previous day, 19th, in Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he in charge there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was in charge of his -- of his own people, the JNA people from the normal army, which also were a kind of guard for the EC members, and the EC members, it was, the agreement was that it was only me and my interpreter, Petr Kypr, that were able to go to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Sljivancanin give any reason why you could not proceed to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He said that it was too dangerous, that there were snipers in the streets, and they had to clean up before we reached the hospital. We go there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able, from your position at the bridge, to see down the road into the direction of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see any signs of fighting, any sniper activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there were no fighting. People were just walking around, or not people, the soldiers, the Serbian regular soldiers were walking around in the streets and some of them are firing, celebrating in the air with their guns.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of them, the soldiers you have just described, appear to be taking cover or any other kind of protective measures, being concerned about snipers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the gunfire you heard, that was what you described as celebration --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Celebration fire, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any other members of the humanitarian organisations try to pass into the direction of the hospital as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When we are stopped there, maybe half an hour later, the chief from the Red Cross arrived and tried to reach the hospital again, and had -- you could call it a conversation with Major Sljivancanin where they were shouting at each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was this representative of the ICRC successful in arguing about access to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. He was told that they could not trust the Red Cross, and when we reached the hospital, the ECMM, or me, I was in charge of these humanitarian...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were eventually able to pass through this checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, I think we stay at the checkpoint about two hours or something like that and then we were able to go to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at the hospital, what did you observe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I observed that the hospital was -- had been more damaged since last time, and in the hospital, or around the hospital there were three kinds of soldiers. Of course, our protection guard from the JNA, and there were reservist soldiers, and then there were these irregular soldiers, and they were just walking around and some of them were beating the patients that were laying on the floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Sljivancanin around there in the hospital as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In terms of the patients, did you see any patients?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I saw all the patients, and I walked around with a doctor from the Red Cross and made a list about all of the patients to the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These patients, were they recently wounded, or were the wounds older in your judgement, as a doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was at least one week old.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So no recent wounds. Previous days or so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No recent wounds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the unwounded civilians looking like? Were there women, kids, men? Can you describe it for us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the hospital staff or the civilians were outside the building and there were women and there were children and of course there was some men too, but later I understand that these were the men that decided to go to Serbia after the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which were only a few, I assume.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you talk to one or two of those civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I talked with, I think she was a dentist, a doctor, which I had been talking to one month before, but she had said nothing about what has happened. I think she was really scared at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to evacuate any patients or other civilians from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think after an hour the JNA came with, I think, 10 ambulances and I think four buses or something like that, civilian buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you join these buses provided by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I was told that I was only monitoring, and I could not do anything myself, just watch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In terms of timing, when did -- did you see the convoy leaving the hospital and what time was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was just before dark, the convoy leave the hospital, and at that time it was, I think, or I was told that it was taken over by our original group of ECMM members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you stayed all afternoon in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I went also to the, I think it was a school or a hospital or -- in another town where we stayed with a patient, the night over, and then the next day I went back to Vukovar to get the last of the wounded people out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you did not see the convoy leaving in the afternoon, or you said evening of the 20th November.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw the convoy leaving from the hospital, yes, and I was also told from the other ECMM members that some of the buses were entered by some Serbs, which they tried to scare the people in them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you eventually return back, out of this area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 21st November we had -- we take the last patient out of the hospital and then we were travelling to Bosnia, and that way around, back to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: At this point I would like to show to you a brief video clip. For your Honours and the Defence, I have a transcript in both English and the original language which is a mixture between English and the local languages. Each of the transcripts has four pages, the first four being the original, and then the second four pages, the English translation. I might ask you at this point, did you hear later that you did not collect all the people from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When we reached the hospital on 20th, we hear that -- and the major also tell us that they had taken some prisoners away from the hospital, yes. And of course also the Dr. Bosanac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You mentioned her already. Thank you very much. If the technicians could get prepared, please... (Video played) Maybe can we quickly stop here? Doctor, do you remember this scene here you have just seen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was 2 metres or 3 metres from that conversation there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which location is it? Is it the bridge over the Vuka River you described a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It is just beneath the bridge and we saw the bridge and we saw the APC on the bridge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we can have the picture of this video, the still picture now on the monitor, please -- excuse me, if I may ask the technicians, can we have the video, the still picture on the monitor, the monitor on our video, I mean, on our desks so that the witness is able to -- exactly. Yes. So we could proceed with it until we see the persons involved in that conversation, if the technicians can go on with the video, please: if you can stop now, please. Thank you very much. Dr. Schou, can you describe for us now the two persons we see on this -- you just saw a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I can -- the two persons, they are the leader of the Red Cross, the person to the right, and to the -- oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the other person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the other person is Major Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now we can proceed with the video. (Video played)

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: (videotape translated). I got used to better collaboration with the JNA than what I am getting today... What is the matter? The colonel knows all the problems. No, there aren't any problems. It's just... The problem is... I can see soldiers walking on the streets. I can see the trucks going in. Look. Look. Look. There. Well, now I have opened the bridge to traffic... That bridge was not open to traffic. My colleagues were there. If, sir, your only concern are the interests of the people who are in that cellar and who my soldiers are keeping safe in that case that is all taken care of. If that is no concern of yours, then I have had young soldiers killed, 18, 19 and 20 years olds, then you are not welcome here. And, sir, my own soldiers have been killed here tonight and, sir, there is a war on here. My soldiers got killed here tonight as well, and there is a war here, sir. I know. We are trying to make sure that you are all safe and left in peace, while you are coming to me talking of problems. If you do not like it here feel free to return back and go where you do like it, and I am embarrassed to have you treat me this way. Whatever you asked of me I have given it all. The convoy is moving towards the Vukovar hospital. It is about a kilometre away from the centre of town. This is a street that leads through the centre of town, to the Vukovar hospital. On the right-hand side --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can we stop the video for a second, please? Can you describe the scene now for us, Doctor? What is happening now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now we are travelling to the hospital, and in the front of us there is the security people with an APC, and then our liaison officer in the white car and then the next car is the ECMM car where I am in, together with Kypr.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we proceed with the video, please. (Video played)

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: (videotape translated). On the right-hand side is the police station of the Croatian police. In that building, or rather from that building came some shooting yesterday, and we witnessed the soldiers carrying out a couple of hundred rifles from that building, that the ZNGs and the members of the Croatian police left us. They were fleeing towards the hospital where part of them were hiding. Now they are entering the hospital and the members of the European mission are there too. You are going to take these vehicles --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we can stop the video again, can you describe, Dr. Schou, now, what we just saw a second ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We arrived to the hospital and at that moment, where the people stopped, the Red Cross or the people were told that we were -- we were monitoring, and that we were in charge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now if you look at the monitor, well, it has appeared again, on the left side, that is your --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the right side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is Petr Kypr.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the person in the middle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the middle that is Major Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. It goes on for a few more seconds, the video, if you could proceed until it ends, please. (Video played) (Video translation): You have these signs and those people with Red Cross signs can also get in and no one else. That is to say no one else can pass through.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That is it. For clarification purposes also, talking about the background commentary, it is a footage by the RTV Belgrade news station. I tender this video as the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. The video will be Exhibit 75 and the transcripts, 75A.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Next, I would like to show the witness a photo album, and it is Prosecution exhibit number 8. I could indicate which picture I mean... (Pause) if you could put it onto the ELMO, would I like to ask you, Doctor, whether you recognise this building.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is the hospital before the damage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And -- or maybe after damage, after it has been reconstructed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, maybe, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe to us what you saw when you entered the hospital yard on 20th together with your colleagues and Mr. Sljivancanin, the scene we just saw on the video?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We saw the hospital was totally damaged. We saw a red cross on the roof of the hospital, around there was some dead bodies or something, and the smell of everything. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us where the buses you were referring to in your testimony were standing? The buses which were provided by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the buses, some of the buses were standing here to pick up the hospital staff which were lined up at this point, and the ambulance, military ambulances and some of the buses, I think two of the buses were travelling this way around and down here to get the people out from the basement. (Indicated).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what time in the day are you now describing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am describing in the afternoon, I think, just before it gets dark, or something, in the 20s of November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The last piece I would like to show you are those nine pictures you provided to the OTP yourself: I would like -- yes, the usher, please, to show the first picture already on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just want to say that these pictures which are my pictures, some of them are taken from myself and some from one of the other people that are -- what we changed pictures together when we arrived in Zagreb. So we had all the pictures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A collection of pictures.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could describe to us this first picture, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first picture, it is -- you could call it a graveyard just outside the hospital, just on the other side of the street where there were a hole in the wall, and inside there, all these people were -- all these dead people were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these people are civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These people are civilians. Only civilians, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we please turn to the second picture? Can you describe this picture to us, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It is in October, and it is where this truck hit the mine, and I can see this is -- this person is myself, and that person is from Medicine Without Borders and some of the others are also ECMM monitors. (Indicated).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is now the incident with the mine you have been describing, half an hour ago.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the incident with the mine and the mine hit the car in this -- just this, this side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, if we could turn to the next picture.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a moment, just a moment, I can tell you that the last car, or something like this, this is the point where this press conference was held.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This picture shows Major Sljivancanin, and German ECMM members, and our liaison officer from Belgrade and it is in November, and it is the 19th November. It is our -- “sightseeing” we had just on the 19th, just for the beginning of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Next picture, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is also the sight where we saw all these irregular people, and this is the Danish ECMM members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean by, "irregular people"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean that -- I feel that there were three kinds of soldiers in the -- on the Serbian side. There were the JNA soldiers which were really professional soldiers, then there were these reservists which also were soldiers, but they were wearing older uniforms, but were under command, and then at last there were these irregular, which was all kinds of people, women, men, old, young, and they wear a knife in the boots, you can see a knife here, and they have all kinds of things on their clothes. (Indicated).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And they were not under command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us turn to the next picture. What can we see here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We can see the hospital, yes, and we can see -- and it must be in November because this is the JNA military ambulance we have there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next picture, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And this is the same time. It is also in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The next picture, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And this is the evacuation and it is the evacuation from the basement which I show you, just before, and these soldiers were doing nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what kind of soldiers were those, now? If you return to the three types of soldiers you have just described a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These types of soldiers, they were reservists. They were from a platoon or something like that and the officers and the soldiers were inside the hospital and they were drunk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next picture, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is outside the hospital, and it is where I took the staff from the hospital and the civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they are now waiting to be evacuated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are waiting to be evacuated in the buses, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the buses you mentioned in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Provided by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the last picture, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the same people from another...

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I tender these pictures as the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 76.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That is all, your Honours, from the Prosecution side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila? Cross-examined by MR. FILA

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is just one segment of this testimony that interests the Defence. In view of the fact that there are some differences in the translation in relation to the original, I should like to ask the witness to look at his statement before him in English, and on page 2, or rather page 3 of that statement, second paragraph from the bottom. In connection with what you saw, regarding mortar fire, I think that this is very important. If the witness could explain where he saw Croatian soldiers with arms. Was it in the hospital, in the hospital building, within the hospital grounds, where that mortar was operating from. Perhaps, your Honour, you could put it to the witness in one question so as to avoid us wasting time. I am sure you understand what I am getting at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I am sure the witness can answer your question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I understand the question, and it was in October, this time, the first time I was in Vukovar, and at that time I was guided around in the damaged hospital by the dentist doctor and at that time I hear a mortar, and I think it must be a 60 or 80 millimetres mortar firing from outside the hospital, but inside the hospital area, somewhere, I cannot exactly say that it is there, but it is inside the hospital area, and it is firing from Vukovar out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you see armed soldiers, Croatian armed soldiers? Inside the hospital or within the hospital grounds?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only in the hospital ground. Of course, there were some Croatian soldiers, the leader of the Croatian or something like that, they were showing us around inside the hospital, but only soldiers, the normal soldiers were outside the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any armed soldier inside the hospital? Anyone, even one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think we have negotiation, or talk with some of the leaders, and they were pistols, yes, inside the hospital in the basement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecutor has already asked you, how come that only you have heard the mortar, the 88 millimetre mortar. How can you explain that other people did not hear it? Is it because you have some military experience and other people did not, or do you have another explanation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About the military experience, on that day, there were also other Danish military persons, the ECMM members in the hospital. I can only tell that at that time I was the one that was guided around in the hospital to see how the hospital was on a -- you can call it on a professional view, and I did not know where the other people are at this time. Maybe in the basement together with the Croatian leaders, I did not know it, but I was guided around and see all buildings and see where they operate, the patients, and where they have their medicine and where they make the supply for the wounded and all these things, so I was guided around, and I was the only one that was guided around, outside, you can see in any floor, and... so I cannot explain, I can only tell -- and I also state to the ECMM that I have heard this mortar firing and it is also to the head of mission when I reached Zagreb I tell that I heard a mortar firing from the hospital ground outside -- from Vukovar outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know, of course, that it is not allowed to use weapons within a hospital, and to fire from a hospital.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that and I also know that when I told --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe the witness could answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Which question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I know that you are not allowed to have weapons inside a hospital area, not only in the hospital, it is also in the area of the hospital. I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Waespi?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can I ask an additional question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Of course. Re-examined by MR. WAESPI

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see whether those soldiers who were sort of operating the mortar were JNA forces or forces from the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was inside the hospital area, so of course it must have been the Croatian side that was firing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you saw the mortar itself, the weapon itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not see the mortar. I hear the mortar firing from this hospital area, and my military experience said that it was in the hospital area. It was about 1 or 100 metre, inside 100 metre from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have a couple of questions for you, Dr. Schou. At one point you said that you saw irregular soldiers -- I am quoting your words -- "irregular soldiers beating the patients lying on the floor". This was on the 20th November.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Now, I would like to know from you whether this happened outside or inside the hospital.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It happened inside the hospital. It happened in the basement, and it happened when we walked around to register all these wounded, when I was together with the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, and did Major Sljivancanin, or his officers or soldiers, do anything to stop that beating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: And could you please tell me how were the irregular soldiers beating the patients? With any tool, weapon, or with their hands, or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With their boots.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: With their boots?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The patients were lying on the floor in the basement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. And one last question. In the last of the pictures -- do you have the pictures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You can see, just the last one, you can see two soldiers together with the civilians. Now, how would you place -- in which category of military people would you place those two soldiers? Remember, the three categories, JNA, reservists and irregulars.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Let us look at the one at the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. These two soldiers, they are what I call reservists and they are from the -- you can call it hospital unit from the logistics, JNA troops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Is there any objection to the witness being released? No objection. Thank you so much, Dr. Schou, for coming here to give evidence in court. You may now be released. Mr. Niemann, should we take a recess now, or probably so that we can start with the new witness. Who is the witness who is here? So can we maybe have a recess of twenty minutes so we will convene at 11.05: (10.45 am) (A short break) (11.05 am)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Please make the solemn declaration. MATE BRLETIC (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Mr. Niemann? Examined by MR. NIEMANN

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases. Would you please state your full name, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mate Brletic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is your date of birth, Mr. Brletic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 13th July 1940.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brletic, on 8th November 1995, were you visited by Mr. Kevin Curtis of the Office of the Prosecutor of the Tribunal, and asked to provide a statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that statement taken down in the English language and then translated to you in the Croatian language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when this process had been complete were you asked to affix your signature to the bottom of each page of that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, I have two copies of each here, one of the original and one of the translation in the Croatian. Could the translation and the original be given to Mr. Fila and ones marked as exhibit, the translation as exhibit A, next in order for the Prosecution, if your Honours please. I think it is probably the same one as Mr. Fila already has. Mr. Brletic, looking at the document now shown to you in the English language, can you see a signature attached to the bottom of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender the statements, if your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 77 and the Croatian translation, 77A.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Brletic, were you trained as a police officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you do special study in criminology as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you a qualified criminologist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1991 did there come a time when you were the police commander for Ilok?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your area of responsibility as police commander of Ilok?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To keep public order and law in Ilok and the vicinity and also the safety and security of the entire population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at the same time, did you also occupy a military position in Ilok?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a commander of the headquarters for defending the town of Ilok and the surrounding area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the military organisation to which you were attached at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Territorial Defence of the town of Ilok.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were your duties in your military capacity, as opposed to your police capacity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To organise defence from incursions by paramilitaries into the town of Ilok, and surrounding areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to ask you some questions, if I may, about the structure of both these organisations, the police and military, in Vukovar at that time, and I would ask you firstly, with respect to the police, in Vukovar, the opstina of Vukovar, what was the chain of command with respect to the commander of police of Ilok. In other words, who was your immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Vukovar was -- there was a police station and Pole Stipo was head of police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was your commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was police commander of the entire police area of Vukovar, which included Ilok as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your superiors, who was his superior, if we can go up the chain, so to speak? Who did he answer to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior in Zagreb, to the Minister of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did the police have any connection to the municipal authorities in Vukovar? Was there any link to them in this chain of command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were direct links with the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe those links for me please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When security and safety and the territory of the municipality are threatened then the president of the municipality ask the police to intervene and to ensure this safety and security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, in certain circumstances does the president of the municipality have a role in terms of commanding the police forces of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. But with the previous approval of the Ministry of the Interior in Zagreb. Then they agree on the detail as to how action should be taken in order to ensure safety and security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we can switch over now to the military side, which you were also a commander of, what about that structure? Who was your immediate superior in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The superior in the military structure was the head of the defence secretariat in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the defence secretariat, what is that body? Can you describe that for us, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The secretariat for national defence falls directly under the Ministry of Defence of the Republic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, is there any link to the municipality authorities, the municipal authorities, with respect to the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are direct links, because in the structure of the municipality that is where the Ministry -- that is where the secretariat of the interior and the secretariat of the defence, they are also at a given point in time the authorities of the municipality, and when there is a safety and security threat in the municipality, then the president of the municipality coordinates this, but according to the command of the Ministry of the Interior and the Ministry of Defence; coordinates the work of these agencies and also coordinates various police and military actions in the territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we can move on to another body and ask what its relationship to the Territorial Defence is; the JNA. How did you understand the link and connection between the JNA and the Territorial Defence?, if there was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is a rather firm link between the JNA and the Territorial Defence. They closely cooperated because in the Territorial Defence there are reserve officers of the JNA who co-ordinated their plans and programmes for the defence of certain municipalities and beyond that, state-wide.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when it comes to mobilisation power, who has the power to mobilise the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mobilisation is carried out through the municipality concerned, where the secretariat for defence is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what role, if any, would the president of the municipality have in relation to the issue of mobilisation of the Territorial Defence?
