utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He actually issues the order commanding mobilisation of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in terms of weapons, who has the authority or responsibility to acquire weapons on behalf of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence, as far as weapons are concerned, is directly related to the Ministry of Defence of the Republic and of the state at large.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in this case, prior to the dissolution of the SFRY it would have been Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would have been Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And generally speaking, would it be fair to say that Croatia, the Republic of Croatia, would have considered that if it came to a question of determining ownership of these weapons, that it, in fact, owned the weapons of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that they could -- there could be a grievance by the Republic of Croatia, under the old federation structure, if the JNA were to take command of those weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the JNA in fact take possession of the weapons of the Territorial Defence, in the Vukovar municipality, so far as you are aware?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The JNA took possession of all the weapons of the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Croatia in 1990 and the Territorial Defence remained without any weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And having regard to the structure of things, and the authorities of the various republics versus the federal authorities, was this considered to be either an inappropriate or an illegal act?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was planned, in good time, and all the weapons were withdrawn because the state of Yugoslavia was afraid that the Territorial Defence would be that strong that it would resist the Yugoslav army, and that is why the weapons were withdrawn to the warehouses of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Having regard to these twin structures, the JNA and the Territorial Defence, was it ever envisaged that one army would turn upon the other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I would like to, if I may, take you to the events in Ilok when you were police commander and when there was an increasing tension between the Serbian side, if I can call it that, and the Croatian side in the Vukovar area and in particular in Ilok. Can you tell us how these events escalated and from when, and the circumstances that led to their escalation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 2nd May 1991 there was an incident at Borovo Selo. The forces, the paramilitary forces, Serb paramilitary forces attacked the MUP forces from Vinkovci when 12 policemen were killed in the area, because of the fear of paramilitaries that they would attack the entire area, in this area where I had command. An issue was ordered to block all roads of the entire border area towards Serbia, and to take the bridge on the Danube River. When we did that, two days later a new order came from the Republic, from the Ministry of the Interior; we deblocked the entire area. On 7th May 1991 the Yugoslav army took all the bridges on the Danube by Batina Skela and all the way up to Ilok and remained permanently in that area and in the area of Croatia. But on the Ilok bridge on one side and the other they are there. The commanders in Backa Palanka and below the bridge are the navy of the Yugoslav army with heavy weapons, Howitzers, guns, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, in effect, your action to, in effect, defend the police which were under attack was met by resistance by the JNA, and the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what happened after that, particularly in the Ilok area? Did the JNA make any further moves or did it just merely move in its forces and stay in position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As tension was mounting, mutual tensions among the population, this had a psychological effect on the entire population, and it was force that was practically advocated. We had to think about this, how to line up our own forces if there was an attack on the city and if they tried to break into the city, how we could repel this. We did not want a conflict with the Yugoslav army, we actually wanted to have full cooperation with them, but on 8th July there was an incident on the bridge, when the Yugoslav forces started firing from tanks, at a police vehicle in which there were four policemen, traffic policemen, who were controlling the police -- the traffic towards Sid. One policeman was killed in this vehicle and three were heavily wounded and they were taken to the Vukovar hospital in order to receive treatment. In this incident the forces of the Territorial Defence or the reservists of the National Guards Corps of Ilok, they resisted and, of course, they destroyed one tank of the Yugoslav army. This was in the early evening around 7 pm and it lasted about until 9 pm. At one point, though, Yugoslav army withdrew from the bridge. We did not take the bridge because we did not have such strong forces. During the night the Yugoslav army took advantage of what they had, and they got into the town of Ilok, a kilometre and a half. That is to say, from the bridge to the Dunav restaurant. This is one and a half kilometres, and that is how they weakened our position, so we were even more jeopardised. And on 8th in the morning, the 8th of July, around 2 pm, aircraft of the Yugoslav army attacked Principovac and bombed it where the military barracks of the ZNG were, and two guards were killed and two were wounded, and this made the situation in Ilok ever more complex and tensions were mounting, vis-à-vis the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, in effect, what you had was the Territorial Defence of Ilok and the police of Ilok, of which you commanded both, in conflict at this stage with the JNA both in its naval, air and ground forces.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, by August, what had happened in the Ilok area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 20th July the Yugoslav army started practically a general attack at 5 am using all weapons. They attacked Ilok, and several facilities were destroyed and a woman was wounded. The attack went on for about two hours. We repelled that attack, soldiers did not enter the town, and we remained in the same positions, the Yugoslav army on the bridge and we near the bridge. I must tell you, the Croat forces were very poorly armed. We hardly had 300 rifles. Out of them, 200 automatic rifles and 100 shotguns and we did not -- we could not effectively resist the Yugoslav army. We were forced to talk to them in order to maintain the territorial integrity of the entire area. The army provoked this. They wanted a conflict because they felt that we were weak, although there was an incredible propaganda among the army. The Jugo officers, those in charge of propaganda, said that in Ilok there were about 7,000 well-armed soldiers with tanks, rocket-launchers and other weapons, which was not true. They knew that very well, because they were convinced themselves through their own operative links, namely through their spies. On 2nd August, the Yugoslav army penetrated through the border from the direction of Sid, and took a dominant position above Ilok, called Principovac and we were fully blocked that way. They had Ilok as it were in the palm of their hand, and they could have destroyed each and every one of our targets. This is a kilometre and a half away from the town of Ilok.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And by this stage, this was about mid-August, I think, had they taken the town of Sotin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About mid-August the forces of the Yugoslav army penetrated to Vucedol and cut off the road between Vukovar and Sotin and Ilok. A group from Negoslavci, a motorised brigade, a motorised unit, went from Negoslavci to Sotin and then to Vukovar and that is when Sotin fell. The people from Sotin started fleeing towards Ilaca, Berk and Nijemci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned a moment ago, you said, "the Croat forces". Just to clarify that, is that a reference to the police and -- the police of Ilok and the Territorial Defence of which you were the commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Joined forces, joined forces. The police forces and the forces of the Territorial Defence, or rather the reserve ZNG, National Guards Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as a result of this military activity out and around Ilok, and particularly in towns such as Sotin and Lovas, did that have an impact in terms of refugees on Ilok itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those points in time had a decisive effect on the state of mind of the whole population. There was chaos, there was fear. People fled from those villages, because there was a blockade towards Vukovar. It was impossible to reach Vukovar, so they were all withdrawing towards Ilok because Ilok had a population of 6-7,000, but daily the population increased, so that at one point there was as many as 20,000 people in Ilok itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did there come a point in time when you decided that the only course open to you was to have negotiations with the forces that were arranged against you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That situation set in later, towards the end of September when the road, Nijemci-Ilaca was cut off, when we had absolutely no connection left with Croatia, nor could we receive military or any other kind of support. Ilok had no hospital. We just had a medical centre with the three general practitioners who could not provide adequate medical treatment, should a larger scale conflict break out between the Croatian forces and the Yugoslav army. Therefore, we were in a very difficult situation, so we would not be able to treat our wounded if such a conflict were to break out, so that the wounded would have to commit suicide. Our other connection was with the Novi Sad hospital, which meant negotiating with the JNA for our wounded to be taken to the Novi Sad hospital, but this probably would not have been feasible, because each of our wounded persons would have been killed. We were therefore forced to start thinking in a different manner, to try and save Ilok and to create some kind of a free territory there, until the crisis in Yugoslavia was completely unravelled, and it was this that we went to negotiate with the Yugoslav army and the civilian authorities in Backa Palanka and the surrounding area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when did you go to Backa Palanka, if you can remember approximately the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In September I went to Backa Palanka on several occasions. The first negotiations regarding a free Ilok started from Nesetin, Karadordevo, Backa Palanka. In Karadordevo, at a higher level, we had a meeting when the Minister of Agriculture, Mr. Seda, came directly from Vukovar, Colonel Markovski and other officers were discussing the de-blocking of a farm near Vukovar which the army needed for milk supplies. We proposed that we would open up a communication to Sotin, a road, to ensure regular supplies. The army agreed to that but two days later did not respect those agreements, and we did not manage to achieve anything on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you first went to Backa Palanka, did they do anything to you personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to Backa Palanka on several occasions, when I was allowed to pass in cooperation with the JNA because it was in the interest of the Yugoslav army for us to free the road, because it was a roundabout way linking Backa Palanka and Sid, because we were keeping it under joint control and they wanted to use it too to transfer their forces to the battle front in Vukovar, and on one occasion in September when I returned from Vukovar, I was called urgently to a meeting at Backa Palanka, to a bridge, in order to reduce tensions and reach agreement on a cease-fire. Colonel Ostojic captured me on that occasion and took me to the military prison in Paragovo near Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long were you held prisoner there for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was held there for five days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you were released, did you ascertain or obtain certain information about what was said about you while you were in detention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was informed, because I was at the top of the headquarters combining the armed forces of Ilok and the surroundings, at that time there was a general attack on Tovarnik which was very important in the context of the overall defence of the area. The army had planned to capture me in order to carry out the attack unhindered, without meeting any resistance, because in the meantime -- I was in Tovarnik on the 21st. I spoke to the Territorial Defence there and their commander regarding the resistance to be put up. When I returned to Ilok, their operational people heard probably that I had been to Tovarnik and that I would put up resistance with men and weapons in Ilok, so they tricked me and while I was in prison the whole area fell and we were cut off. And by capturing me they also wanted to cause panic among the population, knowing that this would have a psychological effect, and worsen the situation in the whole area among the population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what was the general tactics of the JNA when it came to the taking of these towns? Did it follow a particular pattern and course?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Yugoslav army had recognisable patterns. First it would issue sharp ultimatums if the population and the leadership of the village or the town did not respect them. They would first use heavy artillery to shell the locality, to destroy the facilities and then enter those places. Also, they used psychological methods and the people fled leaving everything behind in the direction of Ilok, thinking it would be safer there because after all it was a town, and they thought that there were larger concentrations of Croatian armed forces and of the police force and members of the National Guard Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, who was the commander in the overall district where you were of the JNA, particularly that you had dealings with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The commander of the Novi Sad Corps was Colonel Petar Grahovac and of the whole area was General Arandelovic, who was based in Sid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have discussions and meetings with both of these people in relation to the situation in Ilok?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were these discussions -- where did they take place generally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All these discussions took place in the territory of Serbia, because Yugoslav officers did not want the negotiations to be conducted in the territory of Croatia, considering that their safety was in jeopardy there, even though we guaranteed complete safety. If I could go into Serbia with my negotiators, then I could provide security for them if they came to negotiate with me in Croatia. But since we were weaker, we had to concede. They knew they were stronger than us and they knew that we had to do as they said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to dealing with military officers from the Yugoslav People's Army, were any other officials or persons involved in these negotiations that you attended?, from the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On behalf of Backa Palanka the president of the municipality, Ljubo Novakovic, Mr. Mihael Kertes, their secretary of internal affairs called Dokic and some others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, these other persons, what was their position in the local community affairs, what rank or title did they have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Ljubo Novakovic was president of the town of Backa Palanka, whereas Mr. Kertes held a prominent position in the ruling socialist party of Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, are you able to explain why it is that the president of the Backa Palanka municipality would have any role in these discussions in relation to Ilok. What function did he perform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was directly linked to the Territorial Defence of Backa Palanka, and it is normal for the territory of Backa Palanka -- there was the headquarters of the Motorised Corps of Novi Sad, and JNA soldiers collaborated closely with the mayor because he was their host, in a sense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so, are you saying that there was, in fact, in effect, a joint exercise going on between the JNA and the Territorial Defence of Backa Palanka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because the Yugoslav army additionally supplied the Territorial Defence of Backa Palanka with weapons, because at one point in time they were preparing for a general attack in the territory of Croatia, that is Ilok. They wanted to carry out an invasion across the Danube. They were preparing combat boats in support of the Yugoslav army so that jointly they would capture and carry out a joint-planned attack when the time came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what was the substance of these negotiations? What did you discuss and what was being proposed on either side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The substance of the negotiations had to do almost regularly with ways of protecting the area of Ilok, for the conflicts to cease until the crisis has been overcome. When the tensions heightened to such a pitch and when the Yugoslav army had already captured a number of villages around the town of Ilok, when certain crimes had already been committed against the civilian population, through our intelligence we learned what was in the offing for the town as a whole, and judging by threats and ultimatums from the Yugoslav army and officers who were planning to attack with every weapon at their disposal, we learned that the encirclement was tightening. In fact there were three encirclements. Strong forces had been brought in. 15-20,000 troops, Territorial Defence units and regular army units with all the possible weapons, combat boats, more than 200 tanks and we do not even know the number of artillery pieces -- so in those negotiations we asked that we be allowed and permitted a general crime to be prevented from happening in Ilok because the population and the town would be totally destroyed, and the economy, because the whole town is concentrated on 4 square kilometres, each shell has its target, and the little armed forces that Ilok had, would, of course, resist the enemy. How long that resistance would last, one cannot tell, and the Yugoslav army wanted that, wanted to take advantage of that, and the whole population would have been destroyed, and that is why we proposed at those meetings, that they make it possible for us to carry out an exodus of the population because, according to the Geneva Conventions, the population has a right to this. However, this was not immediately -- this did not immediately bear fruit, because higher level commands had to be consulted, and these things had to be discussed on several occasions. When we had agreed on the models, then this proposal was addressed through senior army officers to Dragolujb Arandelovic, with whom we had agreed a meeting at which we would agree on the method, and see whether the Yugoslav army would allow us to leave Ilok together with the entire population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the Geneva Conventions ever specifically mentioned and discussed at these meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Rarely were the Geneva Conventions mentioned. The delegation of Ilok did mention that we had the right to this, whereas the Yugoslav officer said, "you know what you can do with that, right? We are the ones who are determining what is right".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall an occasion on 26th September of 1991 being contacted by Colonel Grahovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do. It was between the 26th and 30th September. The telephone rang, and my policemen informed me that I was wanted urgently by Colonel Grahovac. This must have been in the morning between 9 and 11. He asked me to come to Backa Palanka, that a European Mission had arrived, or rather the European Monitors who wanted to see for themselves what was happening in the territory of the town of Ilok and the surroundings. Since they were afraid of entering the town of Ilok where allegedly war operations were under way and the Yugoslav army could not guarantee their safety across the bridge, I was asked to come personally in a police car to Backa Palanka to give them assurances and to transport them to the town of Ilok.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened? When did you go -- what time of the morning was this, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was happening between 9 o'clock and 11 o'clock in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened? You went there and what occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I got there in my car, or rather when I left the police station, the town of Ilok was full of people, people were outside, they had already learned that the European Monitoring Mission was in Backa Palanka, and they were happy believing that they would bring salvation. They would inform Europe, and the tensions and the siege of Ilok would be stopped, and that the JNA would withdraw. When I crossed the bridge in my police car and came out in front of Mr. Grahovac's headquarters we greeted each other, we met the Monitors, there was a whole line of civilian personages, some of them I knew, some I did not. Among them was Mr. Dokmanovic, the president of the municipal assembly of Vukovar. When I approached him I offered my hand, he refused to shake hands with me. I was embarrassed. I ignored it. I said, "Mr. Slavko, it could be a good idea for you to come to Ilok and help the suffering people there, to use your influence with the Yugoslav army, not to allow any incursions, to prevent any crime in the territory of Ilok". His answer was that he cannot go to Ilok, that it was an Ustasha stronghold, and he said, "escort me to Vukovar", and I said, "you will be escorted by the Yugoslav army. You can go where you will".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you know -- were you able to ascertain what role Slavko Dokmanovic was playing at this meeting that you were having with the officers of the JNA and the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was even surprised to see Slavko Dokmanovic in Backa Palanka because until then I did not know that he was in that area. I did not quite understand why he was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot really tell you now because I cannot remember whether he was in civilian clothes or in an uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you able to name some of the other people that were there at the time, and give the positions that they held, apart from those which you have already mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have already mentioned Ljubo Novakovic, then Mr. Kertes, with the Yugoslav officers. I did not know the other people. I knew them but I do not know their names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what about the ECMM Monitors. Did you ascertain who they were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think one of them was a Pole, one was a Frenchman and I do not remember who the third one was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what happened after this meeting? Did the ECMM Monitors go back to Ilok with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The Monitors got into their car, I turned my car around and led them towards the police station in Ilok. When we got there, we had talked about the problems, the overall situation in the whole area. By mobile telephone they informed the European Community headquarters and the government of the Republic of Croatia regarding the situation in Ilok.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, near Backa Palanka and particularly the Ilok bridge, did you learn of a place that was used for training volunteers and reservists on the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the area of Backa Palanka, where the Territorial Defence of Backa Palanka was billeted, is a place called Bagremar. In that place was a centre for the collection of volunteers of paramilitary forces of the Republic of Serbia, to be sent to the front in Vukovar. On one occasion, towards the end of September, I was with a police patrol on the road that was controlling the traffic at that intersection. It was in the morning, and from the direction of Backa Palanka a convoy of buses, full of members of paramilitary formations from Serbia was heading to Sid, and from Sid via Tovarnik, Negoslavci, for the battle front in Vukovar. I concluded from this that there was a possibility to explain why Slavko was in the territory of Serbia, because, possibly, he was also involved in the collection of those forces in the territory of Serbia, because there were several collection points in Serbia, not just in Backa Palanka, in Apatin, Sombor and others. We learned all this from our intelligence sources that we had in that area. I cannot claim that any one of my people actually saw Slavko at any point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what happened next in the course of these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The definitive talks when we came to an agreement with General Arandelovic were held in Sid in the command of General Arandelovic. Representatives of the town of Ilok, and the surrounding places Bapska, Sarnitca, Mohovo, Lovas and a part of Tovarnik, a delegation consisting of some fifteen members, accompanied by the Yugo army went to Sid where we were received by General Arandelovic together with his escort of officers, and we spent about five hours negotiating, regarding the evacuation of the entire population from the town of Ilok and the surrounding villages. We agreed on the details, we drew up an agreement, signed it, by both sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was attending this meeting? Who attended this meeting at Sid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Apart from General Arandelovic, there was Colonel Grahovac, Captain Petrovic, Major Mucalovic, Major Banic, Colonel Ostojic, public prosecutor of Sid, who was also the author of the agreement. We could not have much influence over of the agreement because it was dictated by the Yugo army and as it had dominant control over the whole region, and we were happy that they would let our people out, and guarantee their safety, the only thing we managed to achieve was that all members of the reserve of the Guards' Corps should be allowed to leave unhindered, and the police should be the guarantee of a peaceful departure from Ilok, and that it should provide security for the convoy of displaced persons with its weapons and all its material resources.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any discussions or agreements reached with respect to people being taken out, of the evacuations from Ilok?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a discussion, and it was agreed that the evacuation should begin exactly on the 17th of October at 8 o'clock from the bridge on the Danube River, by the town of Ilok.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But, the Croatian forces should surrender their weapons and if we did not meet these conditions, the exodus could not begin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, going back to this large meeting that you had, this large meeting you had in Sid in early October 1991, you mentioned the members of the JNA who were present. Are you able to recall there being any other parties present at this delegation, on the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Colonel Milic Jovanovic was present. I did not mention him. He was head of the counter-intelligence service of the entire army in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any civilian members present that you can recall? You mentioned the prosecutor, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Public prosecutor of the municipality of Sid, but he was dressed in the uniform of a Yugoslav army captain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you think of anyone else at this stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, can you go on from there? You discussed the agreement. There was to be an evacuation on 17th October. What was the next thing that was to occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Yugo army did not agree to this exodus, believing that the forces of Ilok, the joint forces of Ilok were talking the people into leaving, and at that point in time they asked for some kind of a guarantee from us as to why the people were leaving, and it was proposed by the civilian authorities in town to have a referendum carried out, who is in favour of a surrender and who is in favour of an exodus, a complete exodus from the town of Ilok, so around the 13th we had a referendum and about 80 per cent were in favour of exodus and 70 per cent were against a surrender of arms and if the army would not allow us to retreat, then there would be full resistance against the aggressor, namely the Yugoslav army. After we carried out the referendum, through Colonel Grahovac we informed General Arandelovic about the outcome of the referendum, and he ordered the agreement to be carried out, to start with the exodus on the 17th. The Yugoslav officers at that time were trying to postpone the exodus for two or three days. Through the operative links that existed amongst the Yugoslav officers, we came to realise that a general all-out attack on Ilok was supposed to begin on Saturday morning at 5 o'clock. We urgently requested a full observance of the agreement made, and that regardless of all circumstances it begin at 8 o'clock in the morning of 17th October and to have the agreement honoured, and the agreement was honoured, but had we not got out then, had we stayed for another two or three days there would have been a terrible conflict and the entire population would have been destroyed in that area. That was the wish of the Yugoslav officers, of the Yugoslav army and of the paramilitary units that were together with the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, moving forward to the day of the 17th October 1991, was the evacuation -- did it get under way as planned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly at 8 o'clock I came with a truck full of weapons and explosives. Colonel Grahovac, when he was assured that the war booty was in the truck, he allowed the truck to cross over to Backa Palanka. I did not go to Backa Palanka. The driver of the truck and I remained with Grahovac together on the bridge. The booty was handed over to the headquarters of the Territorial Defence in Bagremar. They were not pleased with the booty because they thought that we had a lot more weapons, and high quality weapons at that. At one point in time Colonel Grahovac told me that I had fooled him as far as weapons were concerned, and he was wondering whether he should stop the exodus or not and I said, "Pero, we have to honour what has been agreed upon because General Kadijevic issued orders that the exodus would have to be observed because there was an agreement between the Croatian government and the general headquarters, the general staff". Then Colonel Petar Grahovac opened the bridge and the exodus started and women were on one side and men were separate from them, and they were fully searched at the other end of the bridge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you see any people from the Serbian side on the bridge there that you recognised, on the day of the exodus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the place where the exodus was taking place and where the people were being separated, all the officers of the Yugoslav army that I knew were present. Also, all the high officials of Backa Palanka were present, and among them I noticed Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic. On the bridge I did not talk to Mr. Dokmanovic because I was too busy with other affairs. This was a highly responsible task that I had to carry out then. Before my own eyes the Territorial Defence people and the Yugoslav officers were taking people out of the column, especially if they found a reason to get someone out, to snatch someone. For example, at one point, Colonel Ostojic said, "look up at the church. You have a machine-gun nest up there. Go up there and destroy it or I am going to go up and do something about it", and together with two officers I had to go to the church steeple and I had to do something about it. We climbed up there and we had to see whether there was a machine-gun nest or not. It took about two hours and then they told him, "no, there is nothing up there". And they took over 30 of my people from the column, innocent people at that. They were not even members of the ZNG, of the National Guards Corps or members of the ruling party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, so far as you were aware was this contrary to the agreement that had been concluded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was quite contrary to the agreement, because I was given personal guarantees by General Arandelovic that not a single person would be taken, regardless of whether they were guilty or not, because in the territory of Ilok lives of people of Serb nationality were not threatened and we were not torching houses of persons of Serb ethnicity. We took care of them and no one was harmed, no one was hurt, and no one's safety was endangered in Ilok and they had no reason to snatch people in, to take them to prison. This was genocide, and I think a dominant role had to be played by Mr. Dokmanovic. He was president of the municipality. He was the person who enjoyed a high reputation and he could have had some influences over the officers. He could have said, "do not take these people to prison". They behaved very arrogantly. Practically they were gloating over the fact that they were winning and they were snatching these people away from us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what happened after that, after the people were taken away? Did the convoy go on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The convoy continued, naturally, and people were moving out of Ilok. They were searched, they were taken to Backa Palanka, and I found out their names and surnames through Yugoslav officers whom I knew personally. I managed to get some fifteen people out of prison, but all of those whose names and surnames I did not know, ended up in the camp at Begejci in Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what happened then? What was the next thing that happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At this very place, when people were taken out, they were practically grabbing, seizing all our things. People were driving vehicles that were socially-owned and the army would not allow them to drive these vehicles. These vehicles were seized and people were loaded onto trucks or tractors and they continued towards Sid. At one point I had a very unpleasant verbal duel with Mr. Grahovac. I told him, "if you cannot command your officers, then tie some dogs here". He had really irritated me, and then Mr. Tomic took out his pistol and he said, "Pero, kill this dog. How can you allow him to raise objections to you now?", and Grahovac did not pay much attention to this. He said, "Mate is right, because during that period of time they took one of my vehicles where my personal belongings were and where my personal weapons were and they took it to Backa Palanka", and then he was shouting at him. He said, "Ostojic, why did you allow this vehicle to be seized?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, the convoy continued all the way up to 5 pm when the last citizen who wished to leave left Ilok, and I left at 5.30 pm. It was already dark. There was some shooting around Ilok. This was the scenario of the Yugoslav army, as if somebody were attacking them, and that is when I managed to get the last soldier out. So I went between two lines of Yugoslav soldiers and paramilitary units and the paramilitaries pointed their rifles at me, and Banic and Mucalovic practically as if they wished to execute us, and they were saying, "you banmuc, you are just like the Ustasha Brletic. Once again, if you try to do something we are going to kill you all". Then Major Banic said to Major Grahovac, he said, "it seems that the paramilitary units have overtaken the command", and he said, "yes, it seems that the Chetniks are more important than we are". And then Mr. Grahovac advised me then. He said, "Mate, if you wish, come to our side, go to Novi Sad. You are going to get a four-room apartment and you are going to get rank of colonel", and I said, "where my people go that is where I go too, because I have to take them to free territory in Croatia". He only advised me, because I did not have an escort, to drive without lights on because he said -- it was dark -- and he said that I might be ambushed on the road, and I drove along the road without lights and I reached Principovac. I joined the convoy, and together with the convoy through Sid I came to Lipovac around 8 pm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned seeing Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic on a number of occasions. How long had you known him for, prior to these events in 1991, when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not know each other personally. We knew of each other, because he was active in sports. He was an engineer of agriculture. Often he would come to Ilok, and we would meet at various meetings, for example, at the ruling party meetings in then Yugoslavia, but we did not have any personal contact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these business contacts that you had with Mr. Dokmanovic, and particularly the party meetings, how often would they occur? Are you able to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they were a couple of times a year. These were the so-called municipal committees of all towns.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I will just ask if you can look around the courtroom and can you see Mr. Dokmanovic and if you can, can you point to him and describe where he is located in the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We know each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just describe where he is in the court for the record, if you would, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is sitting at the last table next to the policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila? Cross-examined by MR. FILA

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With the permission of your Honours, Mr. Brletic, you know that Mr. Dokmanovic was president of the municipal assembly of Vukovar. How long did he hold this post and how long was he in the territory of the municipality of Vukovar in 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was probably there until the person in charge was appointed by the government of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was this? This was probably towards the end of July 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, July 1919.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that after that Slavko Dokmanovic was not president of the municipal assembly of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Then this person appointed by the government of Croatia took over, Mr. Bili.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the point in time that you saw him in connection with Ilok, was he president of the municipal assembly of Vukovar or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time he was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were commander of Ilok, under the headquarters, were Serbs leaving Ilok?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I was commander of the headquarters in Ilok they would leave only when they would hear about the attack of the Yugoslav army that was supposed to be staged or that would actually be staged, then they would flee to Backa Palanka after the attack or, if there was no attack, they would go back home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They did not feel jeopardised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did all Croats leave Ilok or did some remain or did some come back afterwards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 80 per cent of Croats left when the exodus took place. The majority of the population that remained were Slovaks and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did some Croats come back afterwards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know about that. The Croats did not go back. Only those who left and who had relatives in Backa Palanka and in Novi Sad, perhaps they came back after the exodus, they came back to Ilok.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as I understood you, in connection with these events around Ilok, if that is the right way to put it, you saw him twice.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Twice.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first time was in Backa Palanka, as you said, and the second time when the exodus started. That is to say, not several times, but twice.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This second time, for how long did you see him, because you said that you went to the belfry to see whether it was -- whether there was a machine-gun nest and you were --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this was nonsensical, but that is what the Yugoslav army asked about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you get to see him and when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not really pay much attention to that. Several times I glanced at all of them, because I could not really talk to them, because I was busy with other matters, concerning the people who were being searched. I had to be next to the Yugoslav officers who had the lists, so that they would not snatch my people away. I did not make personal contact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw him, was it before your people were snatched or after the people were snatched, because you said that you had to go up to the church steeple, so how did you know where he was then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, among all these people, I saw him two or three times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this before they had snatched your people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did not take these people all at once. Throughout the day they tried to take advantage of when I had to go to the town of Ilok or when I had to surrender the town of Ilok, or when I would go to the Slovak house to see whether something had happened. Then people were snatched. They were being snatched all the time. Not all at once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, throughout the negotiations concerning Ilok, did you not see Dokmanovic as an official participant in the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I only saw him in Backa Palanka and then in Ilok on the 17th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But not during negotiations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not during negotiations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the basis of what are you claiming that he had some kind of authority among the JNA when you said yourself that he was not president of the municipal assembly of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When he was president of the municipality of Vukovar, things were getting more complicated, and I think that he knew the people from the Yugoslav army well. He knew the officers, he knew Mr. Ljubo Novakovic, he certainly knew Mr. Kertes because this was his terrain and before also the presidents of the municipalities had cooperated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I may say so, you are simply drawing the conclusion that he must have known them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you do not have immediate knowledge of the fact that he knew them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your intelligence service, in the territory of Serbia, and in the other case, you called them spies and here you are talking about intelligence service. Did your intelligence people tell you about some kind of anti-Croat role, if that is what I may call it, of Mr. Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I did not receive any kind of information of that sort, that they had noticed him in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While he was president of the municipal assembly, did he perhaps invite the army to help the police in Borovo Selo, when those people were killed with an ambush?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice some kind of extremist functions of his, or some kind of speeches that were extremist when he held a post, and what list was he elected on? How was he elected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was on the SDP list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are those extremists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you had the impression that the JNA wanted to break up Ilok, to destroy Ilok, I mean.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not that I had the impression, but I was fully convinced of that, knowing the officers of the Yugoslav army, and the paramilitary units. I exactly came to that conclusion. I was convinced that that is what they wished to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did somebody have some influence over them or did they have their own chain of command, the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They made decisions according to their own chain of command, and their own responsibility. Mr. Fila, can I tell you, at one point in time, General Arandelovic told me personally, "if you do not surrender weapons with all the arms from tanks -- all the arms you have, I am going to use tanks and Howitzers and aircraft and I am going to level Ilok to the ground", and I said, "Mr. General, you have one daughter. If she is there, would you shoot then?". He said, "yes, I would. I am a general and I carry out orders of the general staff. Yes".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did civilian authorities have some kind of influence over them, for example, the former president of the municipal assembly of Vukovar, orders Arandelovic, "do not shoot at them". Come on sir, we grew up in the same country, and you know what the JNA is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So please will you answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The civilian authorities could have had influence over officers and the higher command, regardless. There is an area where a person with a high reputation can, if he or she wishes to do so, prevent an attack because it is not that we invited the Yugo army to surround Ilok, and to carry out war assignments in that area. It was individuals who did that. You were sitting there in Belgrade, so you do not know about all the things that were happening in that area, but afterwards when the Yugo army would pass through the area, then paramilitary forces would come and they committed major atrocities, crimes in that area, and we are all disassociating ourselves from that, but the president of Yugoslavia is not immune against that. He is probably involved in all of that, and he must have found out that crimes were being committed and he should have issued orders to the generals, because it is the president of Republic who is the commander in chief, not the general staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was the president of the SFRY at that time when this was happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time there was a presidency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was president of the presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably Stipe Mesic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do not say "probably"; you know for sure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Stipe Mesic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Stipe Mesic a Serb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, so the Croat, Stipe Mesic, could have ordered the Yugo army not to attack.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Stipe Mesic did order that but he did not have the influence over the Yugo army. He ordered them not to but they did. Did you ever see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Kadijevic is also a Croat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he is not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. His mother is Croat and his father is a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Who was Prime Minister of the SFRY, then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Anto Markovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also a Croat, I hope.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, for sure, and how come he was Prime Minister of Yugoslavia and how come the president of the SFRY did not order the army not to attack Ilok and Slavko Dokmanovic was supposed to tell them not to attack Ilok?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Why are you asking me that when you know very well who ordered it and who had influence over the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it Slavko Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that is what I am asking you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But he could have been one of the protagonists.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: He could have been. That is another question, but, you know, every word you say is important here. You know that the poet Milkovic said, "it was one strong word that killed me". Remember that? Your generation? Thank you. No further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, would you like to re-examine? Re-examined by MR. NIEMANN

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Brletic, when you said you know who was responsible for this, who were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was thinking of the highest officials in the army, and the highest officials in the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was that? The highest in the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think General Kadijevic is responsible who was at the top of the army leadership, then, as a responsible official in the Republic of Serbia, Mr. Milosevic and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have two questions. You said that the first time you met Mr. Dokmanovic -- after the outbreak of hostilities, of course -- was on 26th September 1991, and this was at Backa Palanka, and in response to a question from the Prosecutor you said that you do not -- did not -- you do not remember how he was dressed. Do you remember whether Mr. Dokmanovic played any role in the discussions or negotiations which took place on that day, on the 26th September? Did he speak in that meeting? This is my first question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So he kept silent. He was silent during the discussion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was talking to a group of people over there. He did not participate in my negotiations with Mr. Grahovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was his relationship to Colonel Grahovac who was there? Was he talking to him? Was he next to him? Do you think that he was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he was standing to the side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we move on to the 17th October when you saw him at a different place at Ilok, and if I understood you correctly, you said you saw him on the bridge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Could you tell us what he was doing on the bridge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was an observer like the rest, watching what was happening with the exodus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Was he talking to those people who crossed the bridge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. He was talking to colleagues from Backa Palanka and the other officers, and members, Serb inhabitants of Ilok who were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Was he wearing an uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. That is all. Is there any objection to the witness being released? No objection? Thank you so much for coming. You may now be released. Mr. Niemann, I assume there are no other witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Witness A will be available this afternoon, I understood, your Honour. After the lunchbreak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Would it be better for him to come here tomorrow, because of his illness, or --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I might ask Mr. Williamson to address you, your Honours, because he has been dealing with him directly. I am not familiar with his exact condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, he had indicated that he could go forward this afternoon, or tomorrow, so it is really the preference of the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe it would be better for him to come here tomorrow, so because, in any case, there is another witness we are going to call tomorrow, you are going to call tomorrow, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Very well, your Honour, I will communicate that to him and I am sure there will be no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Therefore we will stand now in recess and we will meet again tomorrow at 9.15 sharp. Thank you. (12.30 pm)
